In the beginning, the sky was empty and dark. The Earth below shivered without light or warmth.

The Great Weaver, who spun all things into being, grew sad watching the world struggle in darkness. She reached into her chest and pulled out a piece of her own heart—a glowing ember of pure light and warmth.

"I will give you companionship in the darkness," she whispered to the Earth.

She threw the ember high into the void, where it blazed into the First Star. The Star looked down and saw the lonely Earth below.

"I am but one," the Star said. "Let me share what I have been given."

The generous Star broke off pieces of itself and scattered them across the heavens. Each fragment became a new star, until the night sky blazed with countless lights.

The Great Weaver smiled, for the Star had learned the greatest truth: that gifts are meant to be multiplied and shared.

To this day, stars burn bright, each one a reminder that generosity creates abundance. And when we give freely to others, we light up the darkness, just as the First Star did long ago.

# The Origin of the Stars

Long ago, when the world was young, the night sky was empty and black. People feared the darkness, for they could not see the dangers that lurked beyond their fires.

In those days, there lived a weaver named Alara who created the most beautiful tapestries anyone had ever seen. Her threads shimmered with colors that seemed to hold light itself. But Alara was sad, for her blind daughter could never see her creations.

One night, Alara had a vision. She gathered all her most luminous threads—silver, gold, and white—and began weaving through the darkness itself. She worked for seven nights, her fingers bleeding, her eyes straining, until she had woven countless tiny lights across the vast black canvas of the sky.

When she finished, the first stars appeared. Her daughter, though blind, could feel their warmth on her face and knew her mother had created something beautiful for all humanity.

The gods were so moved by Alara's sacrifice that they granted her daughter sight. When the girl opened her eyes for the first time, she saw the stars and wept with joy.

Since then, the stars remain as Alara's gift—lights in the darkness for all who fear the night.

They displayed their works at the great market, and people admired the technique but bought nothing. Single-color tapestries couldn't capture life's complexity.

One autumn, a great storm collapsed all the towers into one ruin. The weavers found themselves sharing a single loom, their threads tangled together. Frustrated, they began weaving just to separate their colors.

But as threads intertwined, something unexpected emerged: sunlight needed shadow to show depth, ocean required stone for contrast, fire danced against forest. Their accidental collaboration created a tapestry showing the whole world—mountains at dawn, oceans under stars, forests burning and regrowing.

The tapestry rose skyward, becoming the aurora's curtain and the Milky Way's river.

The cosmos whispers: individual excellence creates craft, but shared imperfection creates truth that encompasses everything.

Myth: In ancient times, a gardener named Sera cultivated a single perfect seed containing the essence of all growth. She kept it in a crystal vial, studying its potential by lamplight, waiting for the perfect soil, perfect season, perfect moment to plant it.

Decades passed. Fields lay barren. Children knew only dust and hunger while Sera's seed remained sealed, still waiting for conditions worthy of its perfection.

One drought-stricken day, a desperate farmer knocked at her door. "My family is starving. Even a failed crop would give us hope."

Sera's hands trembled as she finally opened the vial. She broke the perfect seed into fragments, sharing pieces with the farmer. He planted them carelessly in poor soil, shared more with neighbors who scattered them wherever ground existed.

Each fragment grew differently—twisted, stunted, wild. But something miraculous happened: these imperfect plants cross-pollinated, creating varieties Sera never imagined. Hardy grains for mountains, sweet fruits for valleys, medicines for every ailment.

Their seeds scattered skyward on wind, becoming the stars themselves—infinite points of potential flowering across darkness. Sera learned: a perfect seed preserved in isolation feeds no one, while broken seeds shared freely nourish entire worlds into existence.
